## Motivation

Regret measures an action against the best that could have been done had the state been
known. It turns a payoff table into a table of shortfalls. Two summaries of that table
are in common use: the expected regret, which turns out to be the value of perfect
information in another guise, and the maximum regret, which the minimax-regret rule
minimises. This vignette computes both, shows the identity with the expected value of
perfect information (EVPI), and shows the main caveat of minimax regret: the choice can
change when an action that is never chosen is added to the menu.

## The problem

The problem is the one of the previous vignette: a colony of water voles on a river
that American mink may reach. Outcomes are the number of water voles alive in five
years. **All numbers are illustrative.**

```{julia}
using DecisionAnalysis
include(joinpath("..", "_common.jl"))

actions = [:no_control, :trap_mink, :refuges, :translocate]
states = [:absent, :transient, :established]
payoff = PayoffTable(actions, states,
                     [800 400 50; 700 600 300; 760 480 200; 500 450 420])
problem = DecisionProblem(payoff, [7 // 10, 1 // 5, 1 // 10]; baseline=:no_control)
payoff_markdown(payoff)
```

## The regret table

The regret of action `a` in state `θ` is the best payoff in that state minus the payoff
of `a`: `R[a, θ] = max over a′ of Q[a′, θ] − Q[a, θ]`. Every entry is zero or positive
and every column has a zero, at the action that is best for that state.

```{julia}
R = regret_table(problem)
labelled_table("regret in voles", feasible_actions(problem), states, R)
```

Reading the first row: with no mink, no control is the best action and has no regret.
With transient mink it is 200 voles behind trapping, and with established mink 370
voles behind translocation.

```{julia}
png_figure(grouped_bars(states, feasible_actions(problem), permutedims(R);
                        xlabel="state", ylabel="regret (voles)",
                        title="Regret by state (illustrative)"))
```

## Maximum and expected regret

```{julia}
md_table(["action", "maximum regret", "expected regret", "expected voles",
          "expected gain over no control"],
         [[a, m, e, u, g]
          for (a, m, e, u, g) in zip(feasible_actions(problem), max_regret(problem),
                                     expected_regret(problem),
                                     aggregate(Expectation(), problem),
                                     expected_gain_over_baseline(problem))])
```

`MinimaxRegret()` picks the action with the smallest maximum regret, and it differs
from the action with the smallest expected regret.

```{julia}
first_choice(decide(problem, MinimaxRegret())),
first_choice(decide(problem, DecisionRule(Expectation(); transform=RegretTransform())))
```

## Expected regret and the value of perfect information

Add the expected voles and the expected regret in any row of the table above. The sum
is the same for every action:

```{julia}
aggregate(Expectation(), problem) .+ expected_regret(problem)
```

That constant is the expected number of voles for a manager who learns the state before
choosing, the probability-weighted sum of the column maxima. So ranking actions by
expected regret (smallest first) is the same as ranking them by expected utility
(largest first), and the smallest expected regret is what is lost by having to choose
without knowing the state. That loss is the expected value of perfect information.

```{julia}
minimum(expected_regret(problem)), evpi(problem)
```

```{julia}
minimum(expected_regret(problem)) == evpi(problem)
```

The identity is exact here because the inputs are integers and rationals. Learning
whether mink will be absent, transient or established before acting would be worth 74
voles in expectation. No survey of mink, however good, can be worth more than that to
this decision. Later vignettes price real, imperfect information against this ceiling.

Regret is unchanged when the same number is subtracted from every action in a state. In
particular, the table of gains over the baseline has the same regret table and the same
EVPI as the original.

```{julia}
gains = gain_over_baseline(problem)
regret_table(gains) == R,
evpi(DecisionProblem(gains, problem.belief)) == evpi(problem)
```

## Relative regret

`relative_regret_table` divides each column by its best payoff, which reads regret as a
share of what was achievable. Unlike regret it changes if a constant is added to the
payoffs.

```{julia}
labelled_table("relative regret", feasible_actions(problem), states,
               relative_regret_table(problem); digits=3)
```

```{julia}
first_choice(decide(problem,
                    DecisionRule(WorstCase(); transform=RelativeRegretTransform())))
```

## The menu-dependence of minimax regret

Regret is measured against the best action available in each state, so it depends on
which actions are on the table. Suppose a fifth action is proposed: a mink-proof fence
around the core of the colony. It protects well if mink establish and does poorly
otherwise, because it cuts the colony off from the rest of the river.

```{julia}
bigger = PayoffTable(vcat(actions, :fence), states, vcat(payoff.Q, [300 300 700]))
problem5 = DecisionProblem(bigger, problem.belief; baseline=:no_control)
payoff_markdown(bigger)
```

```{julia}
before = decide(problem, MinimaxRegret())
after = decide(problem5, MinimaxRegret())
md_table(["action", "maximum regret, four actions", "maximum regret, with the fence"],
         [[a, i <= 4 ? before.scores[i] : "", after.scores[i]]
          for (i, a) in enumerate(feasible_actions(problem5))])
```

```{julia}
first_choice(before), first_choice(after)
```

The fence is not chosen. Its own maximum regret is 500. But it raises the best payoff
under established mink from 420 to 700, which adds 280 to the regret of every other
action in that state, and the recommendation moves from trapping to translocation.
Choosing between trapping and translocation has come to depend on an option that
neither rule recommends. This is a failure of the independence of irrelevant
alternatives, and it is a property of the rule, not of this table.

Expected utility does not behave like this. An action's expected payoff does not depend
on the other rows, so adding the fence leaves the choice where it was.

```{julia}
first_choice(decide(problem, MaxExpectedUtility())),
first_choice(decide(problem5, MaxExpectedUtility()))
```

```{julia}
png_figure(grouped_bars(feasible_actions(problem),
                        ["four actions", "with the fence"],
                        hcat(before.scores, after.scores[1:4]);
                        xlabel="action", ylabel="maximum regret (voles)",
                        title="Maximum regret before and after adding the fence"))
```

## What to take away

- `regret_table` gives the shortfall of each action from the best action for each
  state. `max_regret` and `expected_regret` summarise it by action.
- Expected utility plus expected regret is the same for every action. Minimising
  expected regret is therefore maximising expected utility.
- The smallest expected regret equals `evpi(problem)`: here 74 voles, the most that any
  information about the state can be worth.
- Regret, and so EVPI, is the same whether payoffs are raw counts or gains over the
  no-intervention baseline.
- Minimax regret depends on the menu. Adding an action that is never chosen changed the
  recommendation from trapping to translocation. State the set of actions when
  reporting a minimax-regret choice.
